extracted.intended_audience: writers/authors preparing query letters to literary agents (primarily fiction authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on composing an effective one-page query letter to seek literary-agent representation, including structure, required content, personalization, comps, and exceptions for literary and non-fiction projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce the purpose of your letter
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce the purpose of your letter (ie: to secure representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State immediately that you are seeking representation so the agent understands your intent at once. This is part of the one-sentence opener and demonstrates professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define manuscript concisely (title, genre, word count)
rubrics_metrics.description: To define in a very concise way the manuscript that you’ve written (ie: title, genre, word count).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include title (underlined or, better, in italics), approximate genre/territory, and word count rounded to the nearest 5,000 words to show market awareness. Make the information fast and clear so the agent can instantly understand what you’re offering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce the work (setting / setup / premise / main character)
rubrics_metrics.description: To introduce your work at slightly more length – so you say what it is (setting / setup / premise / main character).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 1-2 paragraphs give the essential facts about setting, premise and main character(s). This is not a back-of-book blurb nor a detailed synopsis—aim for clear coordinates that let an agent visualise the book quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey emotional mood and payoff
rubrics_metrics.description: To give a sense of the emotional mood of your work – what is the emotional payoff for the reader?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why a reader will care: the atmosphere, emotional arc, or payoff. The 'why' complements the factual 'what' and helps agents judge reader engagement potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present the book's USP / angle
rubrics_metrics.description: To give a hint of your book’s USP or angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver an elevator-pitch-style reason why the agent 'has to know more'—what makes your book distinct from others with a similar premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help agent understand market via comparable titles and personalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: To help the agent understand where your book would fit in the market by including comparable titles and agent personalisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include 2–3 comparable titles (contemporary, commercially successful if possible), explain why they’re comparable, and optionally say 'readers of X, Y, and Z would love this.' Place comps where they best fit in the letter. Be careful: choose genuinely similar books rather than famous authors you simply admire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Say something brief about the author
rubrics_metrics.description: To say something – not much – about you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep author bio short, human, and relevant. Mention significant writing credentials or a platform only if they meaningfully support the book. Avoid résumé-style lists or weak disclaimers like 'I haven’t had much writing experience.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall structure: opener, 1–2 paragraphs, short bio
rubrics_metrics.description: Most query letters should comprise: Introductory sentence (purpose/title/wordcount/genre), 1–2 paragraphs about your book, and a brief note about you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stick to this compact structure for clarity and professionalism. Exceptions exist (see literary fiction/non-fiction) but for most submissions this structure keeps the letter readable and focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-sentence summary elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1 Sentence Summary must say why you’re writing, include the title (underlined/italics), give word count (rounded to nearest 5,000), and state approximate genre or territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model this sentence on the sample provided if helpful. Being tidy and professional in this single line shows you understand industry expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: If genre is ambiguous, describe the book clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: If your book doesn’t fit neat genre boxes, describe the book in 1–2 sentences instead of forcing a single-genre label.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete plot/setting details to communicate the book’s territory (e.g., historical elements, romance, war aspects) rather than inventing an awkward genre label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and purpose of the 1–2 paragraph introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1-2 Paragraph Introduction should explain what your book is and why a reader will feel compelled to read it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid writing a back-of-book blurb or a detailed synopsis. Use a balance of factual 'what' (settings, premise, characters) and emotional 'why' (feel, atmosphere, payoff). Imagine describing the book conversationally to a friend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparable titles: selection and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Include two or three comparable titles; explain why your book is unique and what it adds to those titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose genuinely similar, contemporaneous, commercially successful titles (ideally from the last two years) to show market fit. Avoid lazy comps (only top bestsellers) and don’t use comps that feel crass or unsophisticated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent personalisation: be brief and specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a specific reason why you chose to query this agent; keep it brief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalisation proves you’ve done research and makes your letter more memorable. Don’t use auto-pilot reasons like 'you represent Famous Author X' unless you can state something genuinely relevant. If you have no specific reason, omit personalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the agent correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the agent’s correct name and preferred form of address (e.g., 'Jenny Smith' rather than a misspelling or wrong variant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check spellings carefully—getting a name wrong is a quick way to annoy an agent. Use a first name like 'Jenny' if that seems normal for that agent, but verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author bio: relevance and brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: About you: give a short, human line or two; include relevant background only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your profession or life experience directly informs the book, mention it briefly. If you have real writing credentials (textbooks, prizes, journalism), state them. Avoid long CV-style bios or weak personal anecdotes that add nothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are writing a series, say so and indicate commitment, but avoid sounding rigid or arrogant about future volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention series potential succinctly (as in the sample). Don’t overclaim (e.g., demanding publisher commitments or listing overly detailed future outlines), as that may turn agents off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length: keep the query to one page
rubrics_metrics.description: Your overall letter should not run to more than one page (exceptions for non-fiction and literary fiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conciseness is valued. For non-fiction with a major platform or high-end literary fiction, you may extend to 1.5–2 pages or include a separate bio/platform document as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary fiction exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are writing genuinely high-end literary fiction, agents may expect discussion of themes and what inspired the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary queries can afford to 'strut' a bit: touch on themes, resonances, and authorial intent to show you can 'walk the talk' as a literary writer. Still be thoughtful and avoid clichéd rambling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-fiction platform exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a remarkable platform (large audience) or extraordinary authority, you must outline it in the query (or a separate bio) and may exceed the one-page rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A platform needs substantial, demonstrable reach (six- or seven-figure audiences) to matter. A website or modest social following is usually insufficient. If you have Nobel-level authority or similar, make that clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include requested materials and follow submission specs
rubrics_metrics.description: Check each agent’s submission requirements (often opening chapters + query letter + synopsis) and supply the materials they ask for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow submission instructions precisely. Typical requested attachments include the first three chapters and a synopsis; enclose these or provide them as specified by the agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread and avoid weak language or mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid weak language, misspellings or grammatical howlers in your query letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors undermine professionalism. Don’t include self-deprecating or apologetic comments about your inexperience—agents judge the manuscript, not your life story. Make the letter demonstrate competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query volume and wait time etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Send your material out to at least 6 agents, preferably more like 10–12, and wait roughly 6–8 weeks for a response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents are busy; expect rejections and slow replies. Querying multiple agents is normal. After 6–8 weeks silence or multiple rejections may indicate issues with fit or quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting rejections and next steps
rubrics_metrics.description: If you get many rejections (10+ or no response after 8 weeks), consider whether you chose wrong agents, have poor query/synopsis, or the book needs more work (the latter being most common).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rejections as diagnostic signals. If the book likely needs improvement, seek third-party editorial advice, revise, and resubmit when stronger. Consider agent-match and critique resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't overstate platform or credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: For non-fiction, be realistic about what counts as a platform; modest social numbers or a website are not sufficient unless truly large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have meaningful audience reach (six/seven figures) or extraordinary credentials (awards, major expertise), present them concretely. Otherwise focus on the book’s merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and tone of comparable titles and personalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparable titles and agent personalisation can go anywhere in the letter, but should be concise and genuinely informative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place these elements where they best contribute to clarity. Avoid forced or clumsy triangulations; use comps to show market fit and personalisation to show research.
